KEY MESSAGE 1...Our stretch of beautiful and mild weather
continues through tomorrow as high pressure dominates the
Northeast. Favorable radiational cooling tonight will also
likely result in fog (dense in spots) late tonight into early
tomorrow morning. Then, our attention turns to a developing coastal
storm for Sunday night into Monday. While the NHC continues to
closely monitor the disturbances off the east coast of Florida
where there is a 50% chance of tropical cyclone development,
this actually not the low that we are monitoring for our coastal
storm. Latest satellite imagery shows a second area of 
convection further east off the coast of the Bahamas which model
and ensemble guidance shows developing into our weekend coastal
storm. As this low becomes better organized tomorrow, it will
likely curve northeastward around the periphery of the large 
scale ridge over the North Atlantic. There is good consensus in
the model guidance that this coastal low will deepen and become
better organized through the weekend as it enters into the 
equatorward entrance region of an anticyclonically curved jet 
over Southern Canada. As it deepens, strong warm air and 
moisture advection to the east of the sfc low will strengthen 
mid-level frontogenesis to its north and east, supporting a band
of heavy rainfall within its deformation zone. Considering 
where this low originates with southerly winds to its east 
maintaining a moisture plume from the tropics, this system will 
be quite moisture rich. Thus, the favorable dynamics at play 
will likely result in heavy rainfall rates within the heavy 
rainfall axis. 

While there is high confidence in heavy rainfall amounts/rates 
occurring, the main area of uncertainty continues to be where 
this axis will occur. Latest deterministic and ensemble guidance
has shifted the sfc low track a bit further east, shifting the 
axis of heavy rain further in southern and eastern New England. 
However, there remains a larger spread in the rainfall amounts 
than we would like to see at this time step. Ensemble clusters 
show that the storm track discrepancies are linked to the 
position and strength of upstream shortwaves over southern 
Canada and downstream ridging over the Atlantic. Should phasing 
in these upstream shortwaves be delayed and the northern stream 
trough remain positively tilted longer, the downstream ridging 
would be stronger and allow the coastal low to track closer to 
the coast. This would allow the heavy rainfall axis to track 
further west and spread further into eastern NY and western New 
England. On the other hand, if the trough is weaker or if they 
phase sooner, the downstream ridging would be flatter/less 
amplified and allow the coastal low to escape further east. The 
cluster analysis still shows a nearly 50/50 split in each of 
these scenarios but with some of the latest eastward shift in 
the 12 UTC deterministic and ensemble guidance, our total 
rainfall amounts have decreased compared to the previous 
forecast but still places the highest rainfall amounts and 
greatest probability for greater than 1 inch of rainfall in the 
mid-Hudson Valley, NW CT and western MA. We also continue to 
show a sharp north/west cut-off in total rainfall amounts 
heading towards and north/west of the Capital District as the 
heavy rain likely misses these areas. While there is medium to 
high confidence in rather high rainfall rates at times Sunday 
night (especially 00-06 UTC Mon), the storm is rather fast 
moving, limiting the duration of the high rainfall rates. Thus, 
the probability for total rainfall amounts exceeding 2 inches 
remain low at only 20-30% and confined to the mid-Hudson Valley,
and western New England. Given these trends, the potential for 
flooding remains low, especially given the very dry antecedent 
conditions. Most of the rain should end by early Monday morning.

KEY MESSAGE 2...Behind the Sunday/Monday coastal storm, a potent
cold front pushes through the Northeast Monday night and ushers
in much cooler temperatures and breezy winds. While temperatures
will be much cooler compared the recent mild stretch, it will 
still be seasonably cool for late November. High pressure then 
builds into the Northeast for Wednesday, giving us dry and 
seasonably cool conditions for what is known as the busiest 
travel day of the year. 

As we head into Thanksgiving Day and Friday, there is a strong 
consensus among the latest ensemble members favoring yet another
coastal storm developing. The main area of uncertainty 
continues to be tied to the storm track as northern and southern
stream shortwave troughs over the Central US and Gulf Coast 
States interact and potentially phase. Just when (and if) this 
interaction occurs will impact the time of arrival of 
precipitation from the developing storm. While uncertainties 
remain regarding the overall storm track, there is a signal
